title: There are some griefs that do not scream.
paragraphs: There are some griefs that do not scream.
They sit quietly beside you while everyone else keeps living.

They eat dinner with you.
Sleep beside you.
Walk into church with you.
Smile in photographs with you.
And nobody notices that something inside you already died.
That was Naomi.

Not the polished Sunday school version.
Not the gentle old woman people reduce her to in cute devotionals.

The real Naomi was shattered.
Disillusioned.
Emotionally exhausted.
Spiritually confused.
And dangerously close to believing God had erased her name from His heart forever.
Most people know Ruth’s story.
Very few understand Naomi’s.
And maybe that is because Naomi’s pain feels too familiar.
Because some of you reading this are secretly asking the same question she was asking:
“Why does it feel like God remembers everybody except me?”
The Book of Ruth opens during one of the darkest national periods in Israel’s history:
“In the days when the judges ruled…” (Ruth 1:1)
That single line carries enormous spiritual weight.
The Hebrew says:

בִּימֵי שְׁפֹט הַשֹּׁפְטִים
(Bimei shefot hashofetim)

Literally:
“In the days of the judging of the judges.”

This was chaos.
Moral collapse.
Spiritual compromise.
National rebellion.
Judges 21:25 tells us:
“Every man did what was right in his own eyes.”
Israel was spiritually decaying.
And famine entered Bethlehem.
That detail matters deeply.
Because Bethlehem in Hebrew is:

בֵּית לֶחֶם
(Bet Lechem)
“House of Bread.”
Imagine the irony.
The House of Bread had no bread.
Sometimes God allows emptiness in places we expected abundance.
That alone destroys some people’s faith.
Naomi’s husband Elimelech decides to leave Bethlehem and move to Moab.
Moab was not spiritually neutral territory.
Moab represented compromise, hostility toward God’s people, and generational rebellion.
Yet desperation pushes the family there anyway.
And then everything collapses.
Elimelech dies.
Then Naomi’s sons die too.
One funeral after another.
One grave after another.
One heartbreak after another.
Until Naomi is left standing in a foreign land with no husband, no sons, no security, no future, and no visible evidence that God still cared.
In ancient Jewish culture, this was catastrophic beyond modern comprehension.
A widow without sons had almost no social protection.

No inheritance security.
No stable provision.
No generational future.
Naomi was not merely grieving emotionally.
She was ruined economically, socially, physically, spiritually, and psychologically.
And this is where Scripture becomes painfully honest.
Ruth 1:20–21 says:
“Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.”
The Hebrew is devastating.

אַל־תִּקְרֶאנָה לִי נָעֳמִי קְרֶאןָ לִי מָרָא
(Al-tiqrena li Na‘omi, qre’na li Mara)

“Do not call me Pleasantness…
Call me Bitter.”
Naomi means “pleasant,” “delightful,” or “sweet.”
Mara means “bitter.”
She literally renames herself according to her pain.
Some of you did the same thing emotionally years ago.
You still use the same legal name…
…but internally, grief renamed you.

Divorce renamed you.
Depression renamed you.
The miscarriage renamed you.
The betrayal renamed you.
The addiction renamed you.
The unanswered prayer renamed you.
The funeral renamed you.
People still call you by your old identity…
…but inside you no longer recognize yourself.
And Naomi says something many believers are too afraid to admit aloud:
“I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty.” — Ruth 1:21
The Hebrew word for “empty” is:

רֵיקָם
(reqam)

Utterly emptied.
Drained.
Depleted.
Vacant.
Not wounded.
Empty.
Naomi did not think God was distracted.
She believed God Himself had turned against her.
“The Almighty has testified against me.”

The Hebrew phrase uses:
שַׁדַּי
(Shaddai)
“The Almighty.”
This matters because Naomi still acknowledges God’s sovereignty even while emotionally drowning.
She does not become atheist.
She becomes heartbroken.
There is a difference.
Some of the deepest faith in Scripture sounds uncomfortable because it is honest.

Job said:
“Though He slay me, yet will I trust Him.” (Job 13:15)

David cried:
“My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1)
Even Jesus quoted those words on the cross:

Ἠλί Ἠλί λιμὰ σαβαχθανί
(Eli Eli lema sabachthani)
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Matthew 27:46)
God is not intimidated by wounded honesty.
Religious performance hides pain.
Biblical faith drags pain directly before God.
And here is the untold part of Naomi’s story most people miss:
God was already rebuilding Naomi’s future while she believed her life was over.
Read that again slowly.

While Naomi was calling herself bitter…
God was positioning Ruth.

While Naomi believed Heaven had abandoned her…
God was orchestrating redemption behind the scenes.

While she thought she returned empty…
she unknowingly carried the beginning of a miracle beside her.
Ruth.
A Moabite widow.
An outsider.
A woman nobody expected God to use.
This is one of the greatest theological reversals in Scripture.
Because the same Moabite lineage associated with shame becomes part of the bloodline of King David…
…and eventually Jesus Christ Himself.
Matthew 1 intentionally includes Ruth in the genealogy of Christ.
That was not accidental.
It was redemption screaming through history.
God was saying:
“I can bring Messiah through broken families too.”
You think your story disqualified you?
Ruth’s story says otherwise.
Naomi could not see redemption yet because grief narrows vision.
Pain creates spiritual tunnel vision.
You stop interpreting life through promise and start interpreting life through wounds.
Some of you are there right now.

You still pray…
but quietly expect disappointment.

You still worship…
but numbness has settled into your bones.

You still attend church…
but secretly feel forgotten by God.
And the terrifying part?
You have become so used to surviving that hope itself feels dangerous now.
Naomi understood that feeling.
But God never stopped writing her story.
The Hebrew concept woven throughout Ruth is גָּאַל (ga’al) — “kinsman redeemer.”
A redeemer was someone who restored what had been lost.

Protected inheritance.
Preserved family.
Recovered future.
Boaz becomes the earthly picture of this redemption.
But ultimately Boaz points toward Christ.
Jesus is our greater Redeemer.
Not symbolic redemption.
Actual redemption.
The Greek word used throughout the New Testament for redemption is:

ἀπολύτρωσις
(apolýtrōsis)

“A release secured by payment.”
“A liberation purchased at cost.”
Jesus did not merely sympathize with human suffering.
He entered it.
Isaiah 53:3 says:
“He was despised and rejected by men; a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.”

The Hebrew phrase:
אִישׁ מַכְאֹבוֹת
(ish mak’ovot)
“Man of pains.”
Jesus understands grief from inside grief.
That matters.
Because some people think God only understands victory.
No.

Christ understands abandonment.
Betrayal.
Loneliness.
Weeping.
Suffering.
Physical agony.
Emotional anguish.
Human rejection.
That is why Hebrews 4:15 says we do not have a High Priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses.
He knows.
Completely.
And Naomi’s ending proves something unforgettable:
Temporary bitterness is not permanent abandonment.
By the end of Ruth, Naomi is no longer empty.
The women tell her:
“Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer.” (Ruth 4:14)
Notice that.

The God Naomi thought abandoned her…
had actually been preserving her all along.
Some of you are interpreting unfinished chapters as final conclusions.
But God often hides resurrection inside seasons that feel like burial.
And maybe the hardest truth of all is this:
Naomi was not healed the moment her suffering started.
Healing unfolded slowly.

Through ordinary days.
Unexpected people.
Quiet provision.
Small mercies.
Field by field.
Conversation by conversation.
Step by step.
That is usually how God works.
Not always through instant rescue…
…but through faithful reconstruction.
And somebody reading this needed permission to stop pretending.
You love God…
…but you are tired.
You worship…
…but your heart feels bruised.
You believe…
…but some nights you still wonder if Heaven remembers your address.
Naomi’s story is for you.
Because Scripture does not hide broken believers.
It tells the truth about them.
And the truth is this:
God’s silence is not proof of God’s absence.
The cross already settled that.
Romans 8:38–39 declares that nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
Nothing.

Not grief.
Not depression.
Not failure.
Not bitterness.
Not seasons of confusion.
Not your lowest night.
And if Naomi could see beyond history for one moment…
I think she would tell you this:
“The chapter where you feel abandoned may actually be the chapter where redemption quietly began.”
Sit with it.
Be honest with God.
Somebody else reading your honesty may realize they are not alone tonight.
And never forget this:
Sometimes God is doing His deepest redemption in the very season you are calling empty.
